result: The study identifies 1,215 amphibian species in trade (17% of all amphibian species), representing almost three times the number previously recorded. This finding is based on combining five data sources: online searches, CITES, LEMIS, IUCN assessments, and literature review.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C49, and C97 collectively establish the main finding of 1,215 traded species. The methodology is clearly described (C22-C23, C70-C73), combining multiple independent data sources (C24-C26, C49, C69) to arrive at this total. The comparison to previous studies (C2, C21) provides context. The data collection and synonym removal process is documented, supporting the validity of this count.

result: Among traded amphibian species, 345 are threatened (22% of traded species, or 28% including Near-Threatened), 100 are Data Deficient or unassessed, and 11% are Endangered or Critically Endangered. The three contemporary data sources detected 157 threatened species.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C29, C54, C55, C66, and C67 provide consistent data on threat status of traded species. The numbers are internally consistent (157 from three sources expanding to 345 when all five sources are included). The percentages align with the total counts. Figure 1 provides visual support. The methodology for assigning IUCN status is described in the mapping section.

result: Analysis of LEMIS data (2000-2014) reveals that 42.3% of amphibians imported into the USA originate from the wild, with 254 of 259 genera impacted by wild capture. On average, 84.2% of individuals per genus come from the wild, with 141 genera exclusively wild-sourced and only five genera fully captive-sourced.
evaluation: Claims C5, C36, C37, C38, C39, C40, and C41 present a coherent analysis of wild vs. captive sourcing from LEMIS data. The percentages are internally consistent (57.2% captive + 42.3% wild + 0.47% other = 100%). The genus-level analysis (C38-C41) is supported by detailed figures (Figure 3 supplements 1-6). The methodology for filtering LEMIS data is described in the Materials and Methods section.

result: Newly described amphibian species (post-1999) can rapidly enter trade, with 38 species detected in the three contemporary inventories and a mean time lag of 6.5±0.78 years between species description and trade appearance. Some species appeared in trade within 1-2 years of description.
evaluation: Claims C6, C44, C45, and C46 present consistent findings on the rapid entry of newly described species into trade. The methodology for determining description dates and trade appearance is described (using Amphibian Species of the World database and temporal analysis). Figure 4 provides visual support. The exclusion of eight species from time lag calculations (appearing only in 2019 snapshot) is appropriately documented. The caveat about potential name updates vs. new exploitation is acknowledged.

result: Traded species origin hotspots include South America, China, and Central Africa. Indonesia dominates global frog leg exports (8,005,997 kg in 2008-2009), with dominant markets in France, Belgium, and the USA.
evaluation: Claims C7, C58, and C92 identify geographic patterns in amphibian trade. The spatial analysis is supported by multiple figures (Figure 2 and supplements) showing species richness and trade patterns. The frog leg export data from UN Comtrade provides specific quantitative evidence for the meat trade dimension. However, the UN Comtrade data is noted to be available only until 2010, which limits temporal assessment of current patterns.

result: CITES regulation covers only 2.4% of all amphibian species (12% of traded species), with coverage varying by data source: 95% of species in CITES trade have appendix listings, but only 14% via LEMIS and 16% via online searches. Coverage by trade purpose ranges from 5% for meat to 18% for medicine.
evaluation: Claims C14, C30, C31, C32, C56, C57, C64, and C96 consistently demonstrate the limited coverage of CITES for amphibian trade. The percentages are internally consistent (2.4% of 8,212 species ≈ 197 species listed, leaving 97.6% unlisted). The variation across data sources (C30-C32) and trade purposes (C57) is well-documented. However, the claim relies on accurate species counts and CITES appendix assignments, which could be affected by taxonomic changes.

result: Traded amphibians are used for multiple purposes: up to 413 species for meat, 805 as pets, 122 for medicine/pharmacological research, and 664 for research or breeding facilities. The methodology for assigning purposes involved keyword analysis of LEMIS importers/exporters and manual verification.
evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C52, and C53 provide counts of species by trade purpose. The methodology section describes the process for categorizing purposes using keywords and manual review, acknowledging uncertainty in some assignments. However, the categories are not mutually exclusive (species can serve multiple purposes), and the text notes that some numbers include local consumption (C50) and species from separate lists (C51). The degree of overlap and potential double-counting is not fully quantified, making the exact interpretation of these numbers uncertain.

result: The online search methodology examined 139 websites across 7,334 pages (2,766 in 2020 snapshot + 4,568 temporal sample), detecting 575 species. Combined with LEMIS (587 species) and CITES (137 species), the three contemporary sources yielded 909 species total, with different sources detecting different species.
evaluation: Claims C22, C23, C24, C25, C26, and C69 describe the data collection methodology and results from contemporary sources. The numbers are internally consistent and the methodology is well-documented in the Materials and Methods section. The finding that different sources detect different species (C69, Figure 6) validates the multi-source approach. The preregistration of the sampling process (mentioned in text) adds credibility.

result: Temporal analysis shows CITES trade remained relatively consistent (around 50 species/year) between 2000-2020, while LEMIS shows an increase to 310 species by 2014. The number of species traded annually may be increasing, though online data shows high interannual variation.
evaluation: Claims C42, C43, and C98 describe temporal trends supported by Figure 3A. The CITES and LEMIS trends are clearly documented. However, the online data shows high variability that correlates with sampling effort (number of pages), and the residual analysis (Figure 3B) is used to infer an underlying increase. The claim that trade may be increasing (C98) is appropriately qualified as uncertain. The LEMIS data limitation (ending in 2014) prevents assessment of more recent trends.

result: English and German language searches detected the most species (293 and 289 respectively) and contained the highest rates of unique species (81 and 97 respectively), despite similar sampling efforts across languages.
evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 are supported by Figure 5, which shows both total species counts and unique species by language. The methodology describes searching in six languages with localized search engines. The finding that German detected more unique species than English despite similar total counts is notable and suggests different market characteristics. The sampling effort (number of websites) is shown in Figure 5 for comparison.

result: The vast majority of amphibian trade is commercial: 99.6% of trade detected across three contemporary sources was commercial, and 99.9% of LEMIS trade (2000-2014) was not from seizure and entered the USA for commercial purposes.
evaluation: Claims C27, C74, and C75 consistently show that amphibian trade is overwhelmingly commercial. The percentages are based on clear categorizations in the data sources. The methodology describes filtering LEMIS data to include only items representing single individuals and categorizing by purpose. The high consistency across different data sources strengthens this finding.

result: Anurans dominated the trade with 729 species, followed by salamanders (162 species) and caecilians (18 species).
evaluation: Claim C28 describes the taxonomic composition of traded species. This finding is straightforward and consistent with the overall species count (729 + 162 + 18 = 909 from three contemporary sources). The dominance of anurans is noted as unsurprising, likely reflecting their greater species diversity overall. Figure 6 provides visual representation of the taxonomic breakdown.

result: The proportion of threatened species varies by data source: 47% of species in CITES trade are threatened, compared to 24% in LEMIS and 23% in online searches. However, due to larger species numbers, LEMIS and online sources account for more total threatened species than CITES.
evaluation: Claims C33, C34, and C35 describe differences in threat status across data sources. The finding that CITES has a higher proportion but lower absolute number of threatened species is logical given CITES focuses on threatened species. The text explicitly notes that relying exclusively on CITES would suggest only 3% of threatened species are traded, whereas LEMIS and Online reveal 5%. This highlights the importance of multiple data sources.

result: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) is attributed to 94 of 159 extinct/potentially extinct amphibian species from the 2008 Global Amphibian Assessment and may be responsible for up to 500 species declines. Rates of Bd in live exports can exceed 60%, with spread linked to pet trade.
evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C61, and C93 are all supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (MacCulloch 2008, Picco and Collins 2008, Scheele et al. 2019, Lambert et al. 2020, Fitzpatrick et al. 2018, Kriger and Hero 2009, Yuan et al. 2018). The text appropriately notes concerns about the 500+ estimate (Lambert et al. 2020). These claims provide important context for the disease risks associated with amphibian trade, though they are based on prior work rather than new findings from this study.

result: Mortality during transit and transport can be as high as 72% in some studies, with amphibian mortality higher than all other groups at 45% within 10 days of confiscation.
evaluation: Claims C62 and C63 are both supported by citation to Ashley et al. 2014. These findings provide important context for understanding that import numbers may underestimate the true impact on wild populations due to mortality before arrival. However, these are findings from prior work, not new data from this study. The text uses these findings to argue that export numbers may be higher than import numbers to compensate for mortality.

result: A recent meta-analysis found abundance declines of 62% (95% CI 20-82%) in traded populations of mammals, birds, and reptiles, but was unable to generate an estimate for amphibians due to lack of standardized studies.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by citation to Morton et al. 2021. This finding provides important context for the potential population impacts of trade, though it explicitly notes the lack of data for amphibians. The text uses this to argue for the need for better baseline population studies and monitoring of amphibian trade impacts. This is prior work, not a new finding from this study.

result: The introduction establishes context from prior work: Aichi targets have been failed, unsustainable wildlife exploitation drives biodiversity loss, amphibians and reptiles are frequently traded with limited CITES coverage, and amphibians show faster population declines than other vertebrates while being sensitive to multiple stressors including trade-related impacts.
evaluation: Claims C8-C21 are all supported by citations to authoritative sources (CBD 2020, IPBES 2019, Herrel and van der Meijden 2014, Marshall et al. 2020, Rowley et al. 2016, Stuart et al. 2004, Hoffmann et al. 2010, and others). These claims establish the context and motivation for the study but are not new findings. They are appropriately cited and provide important background for understanding the significance of the study's results.

result: The World Customs Organization fails to list species data in exports, despite calls for improvements at the 2012 IUCN World Conservation Congress. The 2020 edition failed to address animal trade, and a decade has passed without action on biodiversity conservation in economically oriented databases.
evaluation: Claims C65, C101, C102, and C103 describe regulatory gaps and lack of progress on improving customs data. C101 references a specific IUCN resolution (WCC-2012-Res020), and C102 cites the World Customs Organization 2020 edition. The timeline from 2012 to present (C103) is accurate. These claims support the study's argument for improved monitoring systems, though they describe policy context rather than new empirical findings.

result: The study methodology involved searching websites in six languages (English, French, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Spanish) using Google and Bing, reviewing 1,069 websites with 139 suitable for searching, and using AmphibiaWeb as the taxonomic backbone.
evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C72, and C73 describe methodological details that are clearly documented in the Materials and Methods section. The preregistration of the sampling process (mentioned in text) adds transparency. The decision to expand the search after initial results (C72) is documented. The use of AmphibiaWeb as the taxonomic backbone (C73) is appropriate and clearly stated.

result: Amphibians are sensitive to multiple anthropogenic stressors including pollution, habitat loss, atmospheric changes, introduced pathogens, invasive species, wildlife collection, and agricultural chemicals. These stressors are exacerbated by small distributions and fluctuating populations. Trade is linked to pathogen spread, invasive species, and collection pressures.
evaluation: Claims C76-C87 are all supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Blaustein et al. 2003, Stuart et al. 2004, Lips 2016, Bellard et al. 2016, Phimmachak et al. 2012, Trudeau et al. 2020, Nori et al. 2018, Luo et al. 2015, Hu et al. 2012, Bienentreu and Lesbarrères 2020, Feldmeier et al. 2016, Falaschi et al. 2020, Ribas and Poonlaphdecha 2017, Van Vliet et al. 2017, Onadeko et al. 2011, Auliya et al. 2016, Xiao et al. 2011). These claims establish the biological context for why amphibian trade is concerning but are based on prior work.

result: Prior work has shown that relying on regulator data can miss legal unregulated trade, unregulated harvest poses risks to rare species, meat trade impacts at least 40 Indonesian species annually, bait shop animals carry pathogens and are released, and scientific descriptions can enable species to be targeted for trade.
evaluation: Claims C88, C90, C91, C94, C95, C99, and C100 are all supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Scheffers et al. 2019, Marshall et al. 2020, Auliya et al. 2016, Gratwicke et al. 2010, Picco and Collins 2008, Stringham et al. 2021, Yang and Chan 2015, Yeager et al. 2020). These claims provide important context from prior work that supports the study's arguments about trade risks and monitoring gaps, but they are not new findings from this study.
